title: Vegetables highest in fiber

seo.title: Vegetables highest in fiber
seo.meta_description: Among comparable cooked vegetables, artichoke stands out at about 5.7 g fiber/100 g, followed by collard greens ~4 g, parsnips ~3.6 g and broccoli ~3.3 g. Serving size matters as much as rank.
seo.search_intent: Rank common vegetables by fiber using comparable cooked states and translate the values into realistic servings.

excerpt: Among comparable cooked and drained vegetables, artichoke provides about 5.7 g fiber per 100 g, collard greens about 4.0 g, parsnips 3.6 g, broccoli 3.3 g and cooked carrots around 3.0 g. Those gaps are useful, but the amount you actually eat can matter more than a small difference in rank.
content_html:
Vegetables are not all equally fibrous. One hundred grams of cooked artichoke can provide well over twice the fiber of the same weight of cooked cauliflower. But a useful ranking has to compare similar preparation states and realistic portions.

Cooked vegetables compared per 100 grams

The table uses USDA references for vegetables that are cooked, boiled, drained and without added salt where comparable entries are available.

VegetableFiber per 100 g
Artichoke5.7 g
Collard greens4.0 g
Parsnips3.6 g
Broccoli3.3 g
Carrots3.0 g
Brussels sprouts2.6 g
Cauliflower2.3 g

Artichoke provides about 3.4 g more fiber per 100 g than cauliflower. That is a meaningful concentration difference, but it does not automatically tell you which vegetable adds more fiber to a meal.

Serving size can outrank the ranking

A 150 g serving of cooked artichoke provides roughly 8.6 g fiber. The same weight of broccoli provides about 5.0 g, while 150 g cauliflower provides around 3.5 g.

If you happily eat twice as much of a lower-ranked vegetable, your plate can easily contain more fiber overall.

Why cooking changes per-100-gram numbers

Cooking does not create fiber out of nowhere. Values shift because vegetables gain or lose water and because the edible portion may change. A raw and cooked carrot can therefore show somewhat different fiber concentrations even though the main story is water and weight.

What about green peas?

Cooked green peas are high in fiber and are treated as a vegetable in many meals, but botanically they are legumes. They are left out here so this ranking stays separate from legume comparisons, where their protein and starch profile fits better.

Variety beats chasing one winner

Total dietary fiber usually increases more effectively by eating a mix of vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds than by repeatedly choosing only the number-one vegetable.

The practical takeaway

If you want more fiber from the vegetable part of a meal, artichokes, collard greens, parsnips, broccoli and carrots are especially useful choices. The table tells you concentration; frequency and portion size determine the real contribution.

faq.question: Which vegetable has the most fiber?
faq.answer: Among the cooked vegetables compared here, artichoke leads at about 5.7 g per 100 g.

faq.question: Is broccoli high in fiber?
faq.answer: Cooked and drained broccoli provides about 3.3 g/100 g, or roughly 5 g in a 150 g serving.

faq.question: Why are green peas not in the ranking?
faq.answer: They are often eaten as a vegetable but are botanically legumes, so they are kept with legume comparisons.
